candidates.quote: So death, the most terrifying of ills, is nothing to us, since so long as we exist, death is not with us; but when death comes, then we do not exist.
candidates.author: Epicurus
candidates.locator: section 125, in Epicurus: The Extant Remains
candidates.whyThisMonth: It takes the fear out of the month’s second subject in one breath, so the reader can spend the rest of the day on the first.

candidates.quote: Just as a blind man might find a jewel amongst heaps of rubbish, so this Spirit of Awakening has somehow arisen in me.
candidates.author: Shantideva
candidates.work: A Guide to the Bodhisattva Way of Life (Bodhicaryāvatāra)
candidates.translator: Vesna A. Wallace and B. Alan Wallace, 1997
candidates.whyThisMonth: Pure gratitude for something unearned and unlikely, which is what thanks is when it is honest.

candidates.quote: If man were never to fade away like the dews of Adashino, never to vanish like the smoke over Toribeyama, but lingered on forever in this world, how things would lose their power to move us!
candidates.author: Yoshida Kenkō
candidates.whyThisMonth: It joins the month’s two subjects at the hinge: things move us because they end, so the mortality is the reason for the thanks.

candidates.quote: If we had no winter the spring would not be so pleasant: if we did not sometimes tast of adversity, prosperity would not be so welcome.
candidates.author: Anne Bradstreet
candidates.locator: Meditation XIV, in The Works of Anne Bradstreet in Prose and Verse, ed. John Harvard Ellis (1867), p. 51
candidates.whyThisMonth: A November argument for why the cold months are the ones that teach gratitude, written by a woman for her son.

candidates.quote: Men fear death, as children fear to go in the dark; and as that natural fear in children, is increased with tales, so is the other.
candidates.author: Francis Bacon
candidates.work: Essays or Counsels, Civil and Moral
candidates.locator: ‘Of Death’, the opening sentence, in the edition of 1625
candidates.whyThisMonth: It names the fear and then shrinks it to the size of a child’s dark room, which is the right size for six in the morning.

candidates.quote: I cannot say there is no vanity in making this funeral oration of myself, but I hope it is not a misplaced one; and this is a matter of fact which is easily cleared and ascertained.
candidates.author: David Hume
candidates.locator: the closing sentence, dated 18 April 1776, in The Life of David Hume, Esq. Written by Himself (1777)
candidates.whyThisMonth: A man writing his own obituary a few months before he needed it, cheerful and unfrightened, which is the tone the month wants.

candidates.quote: It is commonly believed that it is difficult to be happy, and there is much reason for such a belief; but it would be much easier for men to be happy if reflecting on and planning conduct preceded action.
candidates.author: Émilie du Châtelet
candidates.locator: the opening sentence, in Selected Philosophical and Scientific Writings (University of Chicago Press, 2009)
candidates.translator: Isabelle Bour and Judith P. Zinsser, 2009
candidates.whyThisMonth: She opens a whole book on happiness by saying it is mostly a matter of thinking first, which gives a grateful morning something to do.

candidates.quote: I am in love with this green earth; the face of town and country; the unspeakable rural solitudes, and the sweet security of streets.
candidates.author: Charles Lamb
candidates.locator: ‘New Year’s Eve’, in The London Magazine, January 1821; collected 1823
candidates.whyThisMonth: A man frankly unwilling to die makes a list of what he would miss, and the list turns out to be the thanksgiving.

candidates.quote: I neither want to die nor do I want to want to die; I want to live for ever and ever and ever.
candidates.author: Miguel de Unamuno
candidates.locator: chapter III, ‘The Hunger of Immortality’, the second clause of the sentence beginning I do not want to die
candidates.whyThisMonth: The unresigned answer to the month, said out loud instead of argued away, and it is a love of living rather than a fear of stopping.

candidates.quote: There is no cure for birth and death save to enjoy the interval.
candidates.author: George Santayana
candidates.work: Soliloquies in England and Later Soliloquies
candidates.whyThisMonth: Twelve words that hold both halves of the month and hand the reader the day itself as the thing to be enjoyed.

candidates.quote: I have often thought it would be a blessing if each human being were stricken blind and deaf for a few days at some time during his early adult life. Darkness would make him more appreciative of sight; silence would teach him the joys of sound.
candidates.author: Helen Keller
candidates.locator: part I, in The Atlantic Monthly, January 1933
candidates.whyThisMonth: The one person with the standing to say it tells the reader that the senses they woke up with are the gift they keep forgetting.

candidates.quote: It seems to me that our three basic needs, for food and security and love, are so mixed and mingled and entwined that we cannot straightly think of one without the others.
candidates.author: M. F. K. Fisher
candidates.whyThisMonth: The month’s table is a thanksgiving table, and this is the sentence that says why eating together is never only eating.

candidates.quote: An individual human existence should be like a river: small at first, narrowly contained within its banks, and rushing passionately past rocks and over waterfalls.
candidates.author: Bertrand Russell
candidates.work: Portraits from Memory and Other Essays
candidates.locator: ‘How to Grow Old’ (George Allen and Unwin, 1956)
candidates.whyThisMonth: An eighty-year-old draws the whole shape of a life as one river, and the drawing consoles before it has even finished.

candidates.quote: To celebrate a festival means: to live out, for some special occasion and in an uncommon manner, the universal assent to the world as a whole.
candidates.author: Josef Pieper
candidates.work: In Tune with the World: A Theory of Festivity
candidates.whyThisMonth: It says what a feast day actually is, which is the theory behind the one holiday this month is built around.

candidates.quote: And so our mothers and grandmothers have, more often than not anonymously, handed on the creative spark, the seed of the flower they themselves never hoped to see: or like a sealed letter they could not plainly read.
candidates.author: Alice Walker
candidates.work: In Search of Our Mothers’ Gardens: Womanist Prose
candidates.locator: the title essay, first in Ms., May 1974; collected by Harcourt Brace Jovanovich, 1983
candidates.whyThisMonth: Thanks addressed to the dead who never saw what they were giving, which is the only kind of gratitude November can still pay.

candidates.quote: In general, the intensity and dedication with which very many human activities are pursued cannot be explained without reference to the awareness that our opportunities are finite, that we cannot choose these activities indefinitely many times.
candidates.author: Martha Nussbaum
candidates.work: Love’s Knowledge: Essays on Philosophy and Literature
candidates.whyThisMonth: It gives the argument the month rests on: the ending is what makes the day worth the effort, not what spoils it.
